sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Danu** ​(*danu*) — ‌Knowledge, Wisdom, ‌Mother of ​the Tuatha ​Dé Danann ​· Knowledge, ​wisdom — ​belongs to ‌the Celtic ​tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Mother ​Goddess, Rivers". ‌The name ​means "Knowledge, ​wisdom"[^1].

**Danu** ​is Ireland’s ​primordial ​mother-goddess: the ‌eponym of ​the Tuatha ‌Dé Danann, ​the ‘peoples ‌of Danu’, ​the divine ‌race who ​came ‌from the ​northern islands ​to take ‌Ireland in ‌the island’s ‌deepest legends. ​She herself ​barely appears ‌in the ​texts ​— her ‌children take ​every scene ​— but ‌the race’s ​name keeps ‌hers, and ​the river-name ​she shares ​with ​the Danube ‌and the ‌Don marks ​her as ‌the Celtic ​river-mother, the ​flowing one ‌beneath the ‌whole family.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name as ‌**Danu** and ​serves its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/danu/). ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— ​a description ‌computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*danu* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed ​by the ‌early domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous ‌written ‌attestation survives ​for ​this ​name; ​**Danu** ​is ‌a scholarly ​transliteration ​of ‌the ​reconstructed ‌spoken ​form. Etymologically ‌the ​name ​means ​"Knowledge, ​wisdom"[^1].

​The ASCII ‌form ​*danu* ‌survives ​only ‌because the ​early ‌domain-name ​system ‌could ​not ​carry diacritics; ‌it ‌is ‌a ​technological ​compromise, ‌not an ​ancient ​spelling. ‌The ​Unicode ​restoration ‌**Danu** recovers ​the ‌full ​diacritic ​detail ​of ​the scholarly ‌transliteration ‌directly ​in ‌the ​address ​bar. The ‌restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent ‌form ‌— ​a ‌description computed ​from ​the ​displayed ‌form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**d** ​→ ​**D** — ‌Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**a** ​→ ‌**a** ​— Same
- ‌**n** ‌→ ​**n** ​— ​Same
- ​**u** → ‌**u** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the name ​is ​**/ˈdɑːnuː/** ​— Reconstructed ​Celtic ​/ Irish ‌transmission.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Dā-** ​— Long ‌ā ​as in ‌“father”; ​the name ​is ​reconstructed ​Proto-Celtic *Dānu.
- ​**-nu** ‌— The ​final ‌u is ​long; ‌the ​name descends ‌from ​the Indo-European ‌river-mother ​*dānu, “the ​flowing ‌one”.
- ‌**** — ‌The ​eponym of ​the ‌Tuatha Dé ​Danann ​— ‌“the peoples ​of ​the goddess ‌Danu”.

​For the ‌modern ​speaker, the ​closest ​approximation ​is: “DAH-noo”

‌Kindred ‌and historical ​forms ‌of the ​name:

- ​**River ‌family** — ‌Danube, ‌Don, Dnieper, ‌Dysna ​— all ‌from ​the ​same *dānu ​root
- ‌**Eponym** — ​the ​Tuatha Dé ​Danann, ‌“the ​peoples of ​Danu”

​The name ‌is ​the same ‌word ​as ‌the Danube ​and ‌the Don ‌— ​the river-mother ​of ​the ​Indo-Europeans, eponym ‌of ‌Ireland’s divine ​race.

sections.body:
**Danu** ​is Ireland’s ‌primordial mother-goddess: ‌the eponym ​of the ​Tuatha ​Dé Danann, ​the ‘peoples ​of Danu’, ‌the divine ​race ​who came ‌from the ​northern islands ‌to take ​Ireland in ‌the ​island’s deepest ​legends. She ​herself barely ​appears in ​the ‌texts — ​her children ‌take every ​scene — ‌but ​the race’s ‌name keeps ​hers, and ‌the river-name ​she ​shares with ‌the Danube ‌and the ‌Don marks ​her ​as the ‌Celtic river-mother, ​the flowing ​one beneath ‌the ​whole family.[^1]

### ​Mother of ‌the Dé ​Danann

The ‌divine race ​bears ​her name ​— the ​Tuatha Dé ‌Danann, the ‌peoples ​of the ‌goddess Danu.

### ​The River-Mother

​Her name ‌is ‌the Indo-European ‌*dānu — ‌the same ​root as ‌the ​Danube, the ​Don, the ​Dnieper.

### The ‌Northern Islands

​Her ​race came ​from four ‌northern cities ​— Falias, ​Murias, ​Gorias, Finias ‌— bearing ​their four ‌treasures.

### Knowledge ​and Wisdom

‌Her ​gifts are ‌the wisdom ‌of the ​race — ​the ​cauldron, the ​spear, the ‌stone, the ‌sword of ​knowledge.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Danu ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**Mother of ​the ​Dé ​Danann** ​— ‌The divine ​race ‌bears ​her ‌name ​— the ‌Tuatha ​Dé ‌Danann, ​the ​peoples of ‌the ‌goddess ‌Danu.
- ​**The ​River-Mother** — ‌Her ​name ​is ‌the ​Indo-European *dānu ​— ‌the ​same ‌root as ​the ​Danube, ​the ​Don, ‌the Dnieper.
- ‌**The ​Northern ‌Islands** ​— ​Her race ‌came ‌from ‌four ‌northern ​cities — ‌Falias, ​Murias, ​Gorias, ​Finias ‌— bearing ​their ​four ​treasures.
- ‌**Knowledge ​and Wisdom** ​— ​Her ‌gifts ​are ‌the wisdom ​of ‌the ​race ‌— ‌the cauldron, ​the ​spear, ​the ​stone, ‌the sword ‌of ​knowledge.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Danu’s mythology is ​peculiar: she is everywhere ‌in the name and ‌nowhere in the stories. ​The Tuatha Dé Danann ​— her peoples — ​fill the Mythological Cycle’s ​battles and sorceries, but ​their mother never takes ‌the stage. Her biography ​is her children’s: the ​coming from the northern islands, ‌the four treasures, the ​battles of Mag Tuired, ‌and the fading into ​the sídhe, the hollow ‌hills where the divine ​race retired when the ​sons of Míl took ​Ireland.[^1]

### The Peoples of ​Danu Arrive (Lebor Gabála)

​The Book of Invasions ‌tells it as history: the ​Tuatha Dé Danann came ‌from the northern islands ​in dark clouds, burned ‌their ships behind them ​on the Irish shore, ‌and contended for the ​island against the Fir ‌Bolg and the Fomoiri. ​From each of the ​four cities they brought ‌a treasure — the stone ‌of Fál, the spear ‌of Lugh, the sword ​of Nuadu, the cauldron ​of the Dagda — ‌the four regalia of ​the divine race, each ​a gift of Danu’s ‌line.[^2]

### The Battles of ​Mag Tuired (Cath Maige ​Tuired)

The race’s great ‌war-cycle pits them against the ​Fomoiri, the sea-demons of ‌chaos: Nuadu’s silver arm, ​Lugh’s many skills, the ​Dagda’s bottomless cauldron, and ​the Morrígan’s prophecy carry ​the day. Danu’s name ‌stands over the whole ‌cycle — the mother’s ​eponym on every battle-line, ‌though she herself never ​draws a sword in the ​telling.

### The Retirement into ‌the Hills (Sídhe Tradition)

‌When the sons of ‌Míl defeated the Dé ‌Danann, the race did ​not die but withdrew ‌— into the sídhe, ​the hollow hills of ​Ireland, where they keep ​their beauty and their ‌treasure and their grievance, and ​from where they still ​interfere, bless, and curse. ​Danu’s peoples became the ‌fairies of Irish tradition; ​their mother’s name contracted ​into the fairy-mounds’ oldest ​title.

### The Danube’s Sister ‌(River-Etymology)

The philology is ​the mythology here: *dānu, ‌‘the flowing one’, names ​rivers from the Danube to ‌the Don to the ​Dnieper — the Indo-European ‌river-mother’s name scattered across ‌the map like water-systems. ​Irish Danu is the ​westernmost daughter of the ​family; her son the ​Dagda’s name has been ‌read as ‘the good ‌god’, the river’s generous ​flood made divine.

sections.label: Irish Mythological Cycles
sections.body:
The Irish mythological cycles — the Mythological, Ulster, Fenian, and Historical Cycles — preserve Danu in medieval manuscript tradition. Texts such as Lebor Gabála and the Táin Bó Cúailnge place the figure within Irish cosmogony and heroic narrative.

The restored form Danu follows normalized Old/Middle Irish orthography.[^1]

sources.citation: Lebor Gabála Érenn (the Book of Invasions).

sections.label: Welsh Sources
sections.body:
Welsh medieval sources, including the Mabinogion and Welsh Triads, preserve cognate or parallel traditions to Danu. These prose tales rework older Celtic material for a Welsh literary audience.

The Unicode restoration Danu preserves the scholarly spelling.[^1]

sources.citation: Lebor Gabála Érenn (the Book of Invasions).

sections.label: Inscriptions & Seals
sections.body:
Inscriptions in Ogham and Latin script occasionally preserve names and epithets from the Celtic world. While direct attestations of Danu are rare, the epigraphic habit confirms the figure's place in the broader insular Celtic landscape.

The restored form Danu serves as the modern scholarly anchor.[^1]
